posts.title: Which Finger Do You Wear Your Engagement Ring On?
posts.headline: On which finger should you wear your engagement ring?
posts.excerpt: Across centuries and across cultures, one quiet ritual has endured: the giving of a ring. Worn as a promise, a bond, a reflection of two lives choosing one path, it has carried many meanings through time. And with each generation, both the way it is worn and the story it tells have gently evolved.

cover.alt: On which finger should you wear your engagement ring?

body.text: The meaning and placement of engagement rings according to Vietnamese and Western cultural beliefs.

Which finger to wear an engagement ring on is a question many couples consider before proposing and preparing for marriage. Wearing a ring, seemingly simple, is actually linked to the meaning, customs, traditions, and culture of each country.

In this article, AURORA will help you understand the proper placement of rings, answer the question of which finger to wear an engagement ring on, and show you how to wear engagement and wedding rings appropriately in modern life while still preserving the meaning of love and commitment.
What is an engagement ring?

An engagement ring is a ring given during an engagement ceremony or proposal, symbolizing a promise of marriage between two people. It's a piece of jewellery with special meaning, marking the transition from a romantic relationship to the stage of preparing for marriage.
Characteristics of engagement rings

items: **Design:**Typically features a diamond or gemstone as the centerpiece, set in a ring of gold, platinum, or other precious metal.

**Wearing an engagement ring:** Most commonly, **it's worn on the ring finger of the left hand** according to Western tradition, or **on the right hand** according to Vietnamese custom (male on the left, female on the right).
**Timing of presentation:** Presented before the official wedding ceremony, during the engagement ceremony, or at a private proposal.

body.alt: Learn about the meaning of wearing rings on each finger.

body.text: The meaning of an engagement ring
A symbol of commitment, representing love.

An engagement ring is a symbol of love, representing a sincere commitment and the desire for a lasting bond between two people. Engagement is not merely a promise, but also an emotional preparation for married life.
To express appreciation.

Choosing and presenting an engagement ring reflects thoughtfulness and sincerity. The meaning of the ring does not lie in its material value, but in the care and intention the giver places into the relationship.
To announce to the community.
The ring also serves as a sign to family, friends, and society that the couple is engaged, and that the wedding ring is simply the next step in their journey of love.
A memorable milestone.
An engagement ring carries the memory of the proposal moment — one of the most important milestones in every couple’s journey.
According to Western tradition, which finger should an engagement ring be worn on?

According to Western tradition, an engagement ring is worn on the ring finger of the left hand. This belief originates from the concept of the “vein of love,” which was thought to run directly from the left ring finger to the heart. Although modern science has disproven this theory, symbolically, the ring finger remains:

items: Symbolizes a lasting bond.
A symbol of love.
Closely associated with marriage.

body.text: In our consultations at Aurora, many clients still choose to purchase a proposal ring and wear their engagement ring on the left hand, as it feels familiar and allows for an easy pairing with the wedding band on the ring finger later on.

body.alt: An engagement ring is worn on the ring finger of the left hand according to Western tradition.

body.text: Which finger do Vietnamese people choose to wear their engagement rings on?
In Vietnam, the choice of which finger to wear a proposal ring on is more flexible and not bound by a single rule. The ring finger – the most popular choice.
Most Vietnamese couples choose to wear the proposal ring on the ring finger, as this position strikes a balance between symbolism and practicality:

items: Easy to pair the engagement ring with a wedding band when entering marriage
Clearly expresses commitment, symbolizing a lasting bond
Suitable for various ring styles, from minimalist to statement designs

body.text: At Aurora, we often encourage our clients to try wearing the ring on both hands to better understand the difference in comfort and feel over time.
Left hand or right hand – which one should you choose?
According to traditional East Asian cultural beliefs:

items: The left hand is associated with emotion
The right hand is associated with action and responsibility

body.text: Therefore:

items: Some people wear the proposal ring on the ring finger of the left hand, influenced by Western tradition
Others wear the proposal ring on the ring finger of the right hand, based on custom or hand dominance

body.text: There is no wrong choice. The finger on which a proposal ring is worn should suit the wearer’s lifestyle and personal habits.
Traditional Vietnamese ring placement: men on the left, women on the right.
Traditionally:

items: Men wear wedding rings on the ring finger of the left hand.
Women wear wedding rings on the ring finger of the right hand.

body.text: In Vietnam, engagement rings are more flexible—there isn’t a single fixed rule about which finger they must be worn on.

body.alt: An engagement ring is worn on the ring finger according to Vietnamese tradition.

body.text: Is it permissible to wear an engagement ring on a finger other than the ring finger?
Absolutely.
Besides the ring finger, some people choose:

items: The middle finger – symbolising stability and responsibility
Or wearing the ring on a necklace, close to the heart

body.text: These choices often come from:

items: Work requirements
Daily lifestyle habits
Feeling uncomfortable wearing a ring on the ring finger

body.text: At Aurora, we always encourage customers to choose the finger that feels most natural to them, rather than forcing themselves to follow a fixed convention.
The meaning of wearing an engagement ring.
For many couples, the meaning of wearing an engagement ring lies in:

items: A serious commitment
A promise toward marriage
A milestone in a mature relationship

body.text: Whether you wear your engagement ring on the ring finger of the left hand, the ring finger of the right hand, or the middle finger, the most important thing is this: you are ready to carry that promise with you every day.
How to wear both an engagement ring and a wedding ring at the same time.
On the wedding day

items: Wear the wedding ring on the ring finger.
The engagement ring can be worn on the other hand or stacked on the outside.

body.text: After marriage
Many couples choose to:

items: Wear only the wedding ring daily.
Wear both the engagement ring and the wedding ring.
Or wear the engagement ring only on special occasions.

body.text: There is no single mandatory way to wear your rings.

body.alt: How to wear an engagement ring and a wedding ring on the ring finger

body.text: Aurora's perspective.
Aurora has encountered many different ways of wearing engagement rings:

items: Some people switch hands after wearing their rings for a few years.
Some people keep their engagement rings as cherished mementos.
Some people wear their rings in a way that feels uniquely their own. You don’t have to follow a trend — choose what feels right for you.

body.text: To us, that is completely natural. A beautiful ring is not defined only by its design, but by the way it becomes part of the wearer’s life.
Frequently Asked Questions (Q&A)
Which finger is most commonly used for wearing an engagement ring? The most common choice is the ring finger, especially the ring finger of the left hand.
Are Vietnamese people required to wear an engagement ring on the right hand? No. Whether it is worn on the left or right hand depends on tradition and personal preference.
Can an engagement ring be worn on the middle finger? Yes. The middle finger is a suitable choice if you feel comfortable wearing it there.
After marriage, is it necessary to continue wearing the engagement ring? Not necessarily. Many people wear only their wedding ring, while the engagement ring is kept as a keepsake.

posts.title: Engagement Ring Design Basics
posts.headline: Ring Design Basics: Understanding Engagement Ring Terminology
posts.excerpt: Our Ring Design Basics blog post breaks down all the essential terminology so you can finally understand what jewelers mean by things like “setting,” “prong,” “halo,” and “pavé.” Whether you’re designing a custom ring or just want to feel more confident browsing, this guide turns confusing vocabulary into simple, clear explanations — making the world of engagement rings way more fun (and way less overwhelming). Dive in and level up your sparkle knowledge!

cover.alt: Buying a oval diamond? Find out about these tips before you do!

body.text: When creating a ring, you'll encounter a world of design language and engagement ring terminology — terms like shank, gallery rail, pavé, basket, and more. To help you feel confident and inspired throughout your design journey, we've curated a clear, beautifully simple guide to what each of these elements means. After reading, you'll have a deeper understanding of the craftsmanship and artistry that bring an engagement ring to life, empowering you to create your dream ring and discover the perfect piece.
Mount

A ring mount, also known as the setting, is the architectural heart of a ring — the entire metal framework that holds and presents the gemstone. The mount plays a crucial role in shaping the ring's appearance, influencing how the gemstone is showcased and the overall aesthetic appeal. It's the bridge between craftsmanship and artistry, determining not only how securely the stone sits but also how the ring catches light, feels on the finger, and expresses style.
Mounts can also be customised with various add-ons, such as decorative features or additional stones, to enhance the ring's appearance further.

body.alt: Explaining the mount on a ring.

body.text: Prongs

Also known as claws, prongs are a type of prong setting—a classic gemstone mounting technique that uses small metal spikes or bars to securely hold the jewel in place while allowing maximum visibility from all angles. Each prong is a slender piece of metal, gently curved over the gemstone, to keep it securely in place, allowing maximum light to enter and enhance its brilliance. Prong settings come in many beautiful variations — from classic four- and six-prong solitaires, to double-claw vintage designs, petal-style prongs that resemble flower tips, and shared-prong settings often seen in elegant diamond bands. This style offers endless design possibilities while showcasing the gemstone as the true centerpiece of the ring.

body.alt: Describing what the prongs are on a ring.

body.text: Tips

The tips are the very ends of the prongs — the small but vital details that hold each gemstone securely in place. Prong tips can be styled in many ways, adding both character and protection to the design. Rounded or ball tips create a soft, classic look, while claw or pointed tips give a refined, elegant finish often seen in modern solitaires. V-shaped tips are used for the corners of gemstones like the princess cut or marquise cut, shielding these shapes from damage. A well-crafted prong setting can also help showcase an eye clean diamond by minimising visible distractions. Over time, these delicate tips naturally wear down through everyday wear, so routine inspection and maintenance are essential to keep the stones safe and secure. Regular servicing ensures the prongs remain strong and the gemstones stay perfectly set for years to come.

body.alt: What are the tips on a ring?

body.text: Accent Stones

Accent stones — also known as side stones — are the smaller gemstones that complement and frame the centre stone. These accent stones come in a variety of shapes, each contributing a unique character to the overall design. Their purpose is to enhance the overall brilliance of the design, drawing the eye toward the focal gem while adding depth, sparkle, and individuality. Side stones can take many forms, from tapered baguettes and trillion cuts to pavé-set diamonds or coloured gemstones for a more distinctive look. Whether subtle or striking, these carefully chosen accents bring balance and artistry to the ring, transforming the centre stone into a complete and harmonious composition. The choice of accent stone shapes can significantly enhance the ring's visual impact, making it more captivating and expressive.

body.alt: Explaining what accent stones are on a engagement ring

body.text: Gallery Rails/Bearing

Most claw-set rings feature a gallery rail — a delicate band of metal positioned between the ring's shoulders, just beneath the centre gemstone. Though often subtle, this structural element plays an essential role: it reinforces the prongs and adds strength to the entire setting, keeping the centre stone secure for decades of wear. Beyond its practical purpose, the gallery rail also offers creative design opportunities. It can be shaped with graceful curves, adorned with filigree detailing, or even set with hidden accent stones for a touch of secret sparkle visible only from the side. A well-crafted gallery rail not only ensures durability but also contributes to the ring's balance, symmetry, and elegance when viewed from every angle.
Some gallery rails can also be personalised with a small engraving, adding a unique and meaningful touch to your ring.

body.alt: Gallery rail on a ring.

body.text: Halo Designs

The halo design is one of the most timeless and radiant styles in engagement rings, celebrated for its ability to enhance brilliance and presence. Originating in the Georgian and Victorian eras, the halo gained prominence during the Art Deco period of the 1920s, when geometric symmetry and glamour defined jewellery design. A traditional halo encircles the centre stone with a ring of smaller diamonds, amplifying sparkle and making the focal gem appear larger. Today, many variations exist — from double halos that add layered brilliance, to hidden halos that sparkle subtly beneath the central stone, and vintage-inspired halos featuring milgrain or coloured accent gems. The halo design remains a perfect balance of elegance and drama, capturing both historical charm and modern sophistication.

body.alt: What is a halo on a ring?

body.text: Shoulders

As the name suggests, the shoulders are the sides of the ring's mount — the elegant curves that rise from the band to support the head and centre stone. Different varieties of shanks can influence the overall design and comfort of the ring, as the shoulders connect directly to the shank, making both elements essential to the ring's structure and style. Their design plays a key role in both structure and style, seamlessly connecting the band to the setting. Shoulders can be crafted in many ways: tapered for a graceful transition, split for an open, modern feel, or adorned with pavé or channel-set stones for extra brilliance. Beyond their visual beauty, well-proportioned shoulders provide balance and stability, ensuring the ring sits comfortably and harmoniously on the hand.

body.alt: The shoulders of the ring.

body.text: Pavé

Pronounced (pa-VAY) is a French word, which literally means "paved" — like a paved street. This technique, developed by French goldsmiths and skilled jewellers, involves setting small diamonds closely together with very little metal between, creating a dazzling effect that is highly valued in fine jewellery. Pavé is a typical style found on many rings today and is a hallmark of craftsmanship in the jewellery world.

body.alt: What is a pave on a ring?

body.text: Bridge

The bridge is part of the ring that sits below the setting and holds the setting and ring together. When planning to stack wedding bands against an engagement ring, the bridge design of the ring is essential to accommodate different styles of wedding bands. The bridge can also be styled with a pave for more sparkle.

body.alt: What is the bridge on an engagement ring?

body.text: Shank

The shank, or the band, is the part that wraps around your finger and is sized accordingly to your finger. At Aurora Saigon, we recommend a shank width of at least 1.8mm to ensure your ring is durable and strong.

body.alt: The shank of the ring.

body.text: Euro Shank

A Euro Shank is a distinctive ring design characterised by a squared or slightly flattened base, as opposed to the traditional round engagement ring band. This subtle geometric shape adds both elegance and functionality, helping to keep the ring upright and preventing it from spinning on the finger, especially for larger or heavier designs. The squared edges also give the ring a contemporary, tailored appearance that balances beautifully with elaborate settings or statement centre stones. Beyond its aesthetic appeal, the Euro Shank offers added comfort and stability, making it a practical choice for those who want their ring to fit securely while maintaining a refined, modern silhouette.

body.alt: euro shank ring design.

body.text: Hidden Halo

Adding a secret sparkle to the ring, hidden halos are placed under or around the basket setting. The hidden halo is our quiet nod to decades of design craft: nothing flashy at first glance, but elegance revealed in every angle. A ring that glows from within—and outside.

body.alt: What is a hidden halo on an engagement ring.

body.text: Cathedral Setting Style

A cathedral setting is a timeless and architectural ring design where the centre diamond is often showcased, with the centre stone gracefully elevated above the band by two arching metal slopes — resembling the sweeping arches of a grand cathedral. These arches elevate the gemstone high, allowing more light to enter and enhance its brilliance, while creating a dramatic and elegant profile. The result is a design that combines classic sophistication with a sense of strength and structure, framing the stone like a masterpiece on display.

body.alt: A picture showing the design style of a cathedral setting style ring.

body.text: Bezel Setting Style

A bezel setting encircles the gemstone with a smooth, custom-fit metal rim that securely holds it in place. The bezel setting covers both the diamond's pavilion and crown, offering protection to the upper and lower portions of the stone. Rather than prongs, the metal surrounds the stone's edges, offering exceptional protection while giving the ring a modern, refined appearance. This design enhances the gem's silhouette, creating a sleek, continuous line between the metal and stone. Loved for its durability and understated elegance, the bezel setting is perfect for those who appreciate clean lines, everyday wearability, and a touch of contemporary sophistication. The bezel setting can also influence light reflection, as the metal rim may affect how light enters and exits the stone, subtly impacting the diamond's overall brilliance.

body.alt: Image of a Bezel style ring to educate what a bezel ring is.

body.text: Hallmark/Engraving

Hallmarking is an ancient practice that traces back to 13th-century England, when goldsmiths were first required to stamp their work with a mark guaranteeing the purity of the metal. This mark — known as a hallmark — assured buyers that the piece met official standards for gold, silver, or platinum. Today, hallmarking remains both a legal requirement in many countries and a symbol of authenticity and craftsmanship.

Alongside hallmarks, engraving adds a deeply personal touch: initials, dates, or messages can be inscribed on the jewellery, transforming it from a beautiful object into a meaningful keepsake. Together, hallmarking and engraving reflect the artistry, integrity, and individuality that define every fine piece of jewellery. A small engraving may also denote a patented cutting style, highlighting the ring's uniqueness and exclusivity.

posts.title: Oval Diamond Buying Advice
posts.headline: What To Look For When Buying an Oval Diamond
posts.excerpt: When purchasing an oval diamond, it's crucial to be well-informed about the specific characteristics that define its quality and beauty. Whether buying an engagement ring or a luxurious piece of jewellery, understanding these aspects can make a significant difference in your selection. Delve into three essential tips you should know before purchasing.

cover.alt: Buying a oval diamond? Find out about these tips before you do!

body.text: When purchasing an oval diamond, it's crucial to be well-informed about the specific characteristics that define its quality and beauty. Whether buying an engagement ring or a luxurious piece of jewellery, understanding these aspects can make a significant difference in your selection. Below, we delve into three essential tips you should know before purchasing.
Avoid Diamonds G or Below on the Colour Scale

One of the most critical factors to consider when buying an oval diamond is its colour. If you desire a truly white diamond, it's advisable to avoid stones that are G or below on the GIA colour scale. The GIA colour scale ranges from D, which is the most colourless, to Z, which is the most yellow. Oval diamonds tend to show colour more prominently, especially towards the tips of the stone. Therefore, selecting a diamond with a higher colour grade ensures that it appears more colourless and vibrant.

body.alt: classic oval diamond engagement ring Ho Chi Minh - Vietnam

body.text: Ideal Ratio for Oval Diamonds: 1.35 to 1.5

The second critical aspect is the length-to-width ratio of the oval diamond. A ratio between 1.35 and 1.5 is considered ideal for achieving a balanced and aesthetically pleasing oval shape. This ratio is calculated by dividing the length measurement of the stone by its width. While you can opt for a ratio above 1.5 for a more elongated look, it's essential to carefully evaluate the stone. A higher ratio might lead to a shallow cut, which can result in windowing, where the diamond loses its brilliance and appears less sparkly.

body.alt: The best ratio for oval diamonds.

body.text: Ovals Without Bow Ties Do Exist

Lastly, many buyers are concerned about the "bow tie" effect that can occur in oval diamonds. This effect is a dark area across the center of the diamond, which can detract from its overall appearance. Fortunately, ovals without bow ties do exist, but they require a different faceting pattern. If you examine the diamond's certificate, stones with certain faceting patterns will exhibit a bow tie, while others will not. Although these diamonds are rarer and often need to be custom cut, they offer a more brilliant and uniform appearance, free from the distracting bow tie effect.

body.alt: Look for bad bow tie effect in oval diamonds.

body.text: Conclusion

Purchasing an oval diamond is a significant investment, and making an informed decision can enhance both the beauty and value of your purchase. By prioritizing a higher colour grade, selecting an ideal ratio, and seeking out diamonds without bow ties, you can ensure that your oval diamond will not only meet but exceed your expectations. With these considerations in mind, you are well on your way to finding the perfect oval diamond that will be cherished for years to come.

posts.title: How Are Diamonds Cut?
posts.headline: The Diamond Cutting Process
posts.excerpt: From the earth's depths to a master's hands, every Diamond Tells a Story, one forged over millions of years by immense heat and pressure. Each facet, angle and polished surface transforms a rough Stone into a radiant gem, unlocking its hidden brilliance. Explore the intricate art of diamond cutting, where science and the craftsman's intuition come together to reveal nature's finest sparkle.

cover.alt: Find out how diamonds are cut.

body.text: From the earth's depths to a master's hands, every Diamond Tells a Story, one forged over millions of years by immense heat and pressure. Each facet, angle and polished surface transforms a rough Stone into a radiant gem, unlocking its hidden brilliance. Explore the intricate art of diamond cutting, where science and the craftsman's intuition come together to reveal nature's finest sparkle.

When a diamond first arrives at a cutting workshop, it is nothing like the gem we picture adorning jewellery in its raw state. It's rugged, irregular, and filled with imperfections and visible inclusions, but inside, there's potential, a spark that only the trained eye and skilled hand of a master cutter can unlock like a sculptor studying a block of marble.
Evaluation and Planning

Each diamond's transformation begins with evaluation and planning. This vital first step sets the course for every step to follow. By using advanced 3D mapping technology, gemologists scan the stone, analyzing every angle, every internal line, and every inclusion. No two diamonds are alike. Each one has a unique map within its structure. This invisible blueprint guides the cutter in deciding the best way to shape the stone and maximize its inherent beauty and market value. It's a balancing act that requires a delicate mix of science and intuition. Sometimes, sacrifices in carrot weight must be made to avoid major inclusions and flaws, while in other cases, strategic adjustments can enhance the diamond's overall clarity and brightness. In this way, cutting becomes a collaborative dance between nature's design and human artistry.

body.alt: Close up of natural rough diamond Ho Chi Minh - Vietnam

body.text: Cleaving and Sawing

Once the diamond map is understood, it's time to divide the rough stone into the cleaving and sawing stages. Cleaving was once a delicate procedure of striking the diamond with a sharp blade, requiring accuracy and a steady hand. Today, however, technology has transformed this process. High-powered lasers have replaced the old methods, allowing cutters to slice through even the hardest diamonds with incredible precision. These lasers emit concentrated beams of light that penetrate the diamond's internal structure along pre-planned paths, creating clean, accurate cuts. By carefully following the diamond's natural grain, the cutter avoids potential cracking or shattering, which could ruin the stone. It's a slow, painstaking procedure, but every detail counts! This is only the beginning of the diamond's journey to brilliance.

body.alt: Diamond jewellery Ho Chi Minh - Vietname

body.text: Bruting

Once divided, the diamond is ready for shaping, known as bruting. This process is where the rough stone takes on its first proper form. The diamond is placed on a lath and spun with its edges ground down by another diamond. Only a diamond can cut another diamond as it's the hardest natural material on earth, ranking ten on the Mohs scale of hardness. Here, brute Force meets precision as the cutter carefully rounds out the stone's edges, creating a symmetrical base shape. This initial shaping is crucial because it establishes the foundation for all subsequent facets. The cutter aims to ensure that every angle aligns to maximize the diamond's future brilliance. Allowing light to travel and reflect in ways that amplify the gem's natural sparkle.

body.alt: diamond in bedrock - Jewellery Ho Chi Minh - Vietname

body.text: Faceting

Next comes faceting, the step that brings the diamond to life by enhancing its capacity for reflection and refraction. Faceting begins with a process called blocking, where the cutter carves out the main facets that define the diamond shape in a round brilliant cut. For example, this initial phase creates eight pavilion facets, eight crown facets, and a large table facet at the top of the stone. These primary facets establish the diamond's basic geometry, but the next phase, brillianteering, adds the finishing touches.

body.alt: anatomy of a round diamond Ho Chi Minh - Vietnam

body.text: Brillianteering

The brillianteering process involves adding smaller facets to increase the diamond's reflectivity. Each facet is cut at a precise angle so that when light enters the stone, it is reflected in a controlled dance across its surface and then exits in a dazzling display of brilliance. The amount of cuts for a round brilliant diamond is 57 or 58 facets, each working in harmony to produce a dazzling array of sparkles. A single misaligned facet can dull the diamond's overall radiance, underscoring the necessity for absolute precision and mastery.

body.alt: diamond Brillianteering Ho Chi Minh - Vietnam

body.text: Polishing

Polishing is the final stage, where the diamond surfaces are refined to create the flawless finish we associate with polished gems. This process smooths out minor imperfections, bringing each facet to a radiant shine using a wheel embedded with diamond powder. A material is as hard as the diamond itself. The cutter polishes every angle, gradually achieving a mirror-like finish that allows the gem to capture light in its purest form. Polishing requires a delicate touch and meticulous attention to detail, as even a slight error could diminish the diamond's ability to reflect light. Every surface is smoothed until the diamond's brilliance is fully realized, creating the vibrant lustre we recognize as the mark of a well-cut stone.

body.alt: Diamond polishing

body.text: Inspection

After polishing, the diamond undergoes a final inspection, during which expert eyes examine every facet angle and surface under magnification. This final check ensures the diamond meets industry standards of symmetry, clarity and polish, which significantly affect its value. The slightest flaw could detract from its overall beauty, making this inspection crucial. Once it passes, the diamond is ready to be graded based on its cut, which encompasses three key criteria. Brilliance fire and scintillation brilliance refer to the white light reflecting within the stone fire, to the rainbow-like dispersion of colours that light produces and scintillation to the diamond's sparkling effect. These qualities form the essence of a diamond's allure and determine its grade when moved together. A well-cut diamond can amplify its natural qualities, masking minor inclusions and colour variances. While a poorly cut diamond, even if flawless, will lack the captivating lustre that makes it desirable.
Conclusion

From an unrefined crystal to a radiant gem, a diamond's journey involves patience, skill and artistry. Each step, evaluation, cleaving, bruting, faceting and polishing, tells the story of craftspeople who have dedicated their lives to revealing the hidden beauty within each stone. It's a journey that begins in the earth's dark depths and ends as a testament to human achievement. In every facet lies a tribute to the cutter's skill, capturing and magnifying the diamond's natural radiance. This is the art and science of diamond cutting, where the world's most cherished stones are born, a legacy of brilliance preserved for generations.

Additionally, they are thought to aid in reducing stress and anxiety, making them a popular choice for those seeking emotional well-being. body.text: This blog post will examine a gorgeous crystal associated with its namesake: Moonstone. This crystal is renowned for its protective properties and for helping with wisdom, passion, and even safe travel.
What is Moonstone?

Moonstone is a beautiful gemstone that belongs to the feldspar mineral group. It is renowned for its soft, shimmering effect reminiscent of moonlight. Moonstone is primarily composed of the mineral Valspar, which is a type of silica mineral. Feldspar is one of the more common minerals in the Earth's crust and is found in various kinds of rock, primarily igneous and metamorphic.

body.alt: Moonstone energy and healing powers.

body.text: Moonstone typically forms within pegmatite-type rock. Pegmatites are coarse-grained igneous rocks that form from the slow cooling of magma deeper than the Earth's crust. These rocks are characterized by their large crystals, which can grow to huge and very impressive sizes due to the slow cooling process that they undergo.

The unique shimmering effect found in Moonstone results from the intergrowth of two types of Valspar minerals within the crystal structure: orthoclase and albite. These minerals cause light to scatter and create the characteristic colours you see from Moonstone.
History and Folklore of Moonstone

Moonstone has a rich history steeped in myth and folklore, spanning various cultures throughout the ages. Its ethereal beauty and captivating luminescence have led to its association with the Moon and its mystical properties. Moonstone has been valued for centuries in cultures all around the world.

For example, it was believed to be a sacred stone in Ancient India and had strong connections to the Moon. Indian mythology associated Moonstone with the moon deity Chandra, and it was considered a symbol of love and fertility. The Romans associated the Moonstone with their lunar goddess, Diana, often invoking its energies to bring about the Moon's blessing and protect against danger during travel at night. Moonstone was also used in Roman jewellery and amulets.

In Arabia, Moonstone was considered a dream stone. It was believed that wearing a Moonstone during a full moon would grant prophetic dreams and visions. Moonstone's colours were thought to resemble the shifting patterns of moonlight through its cycles. In medieval Europe, Moonstone was believed to have protective properties. It was supposed to bring good fortune, enhance intuition, and protect against negative energies. Many would wear Moonstone amulets to ensure a safe journey and promote positive relationships.

In Hindu traditions, Moonstone was considered a sacred gem representing divine feminine energy. It was associated with the goddess of the Moon, and its energies were believed to enhance intuition, psychic abilities, and spiritual insights.
Metaphysical Properties of Moonstone

Moonstone is renowned for its gentle and nurturing energy, making it a popular choice for emotional healing, spiritual growth, and overall well-being. Moonstone is often used to help balance and soothe emotions. It is thought to help calm emotional triggers, reduce stress, and promote inner harmony. It can be particularly beneficial during times of emotional upheaval or change.

cover.alt: Should I buy a lab grown diamond?

body.text: In this blog post, we're diving into the fascinating world of diamonds—specifically, lab-grown diamonds versus natural diamonds. With thousands of questions swirling around, we're here to answer them all. We will guide you through the differences, compare prices, and more. Let's get started!
What is a Lab Grown Diamond?
We always get asked are lab created diamonds real, and the short answer to this is, yes!

Lab diamonds are real diamonds created similarly to natural diamonds, with the same chemical makeup, only in weeks to months. Mined natural diamonds have been created for millions and billions of years. Because of this, there are some differences between the two. But do not make the mistake of calling a lab grown diamond a fake diamond, as they are not fake diamonds. There are in every way visually, chemically and physically identical to a natural diamond.

To the naked eye, distinguishing between lab-grown and natural diamonds is nearly impossible. To detect the differences we will need to look deeper into the creation of the stone and understand how a natural and lab diamond are created. There are differences here that give the game away to detect lab grown diamonds.

body.alt: Lab created diamonds

body.text: How are Lab Diamonds Created?

There are two ways to create diamonds in a lab, but there is only one way to create natural diamonds. One of the lab diamond processes is CVD, which stands for Chemical Vapour Deposition. CVD involves condensing carbon gases onto an existing carbon matrix called a seed under high heat and pressure. The natural diamond process happens when carbon dioxide is trapped in the earth's mantle with intense heat and pressure. The other method to create diamonds in a lab is HPHT, which stands for High Pressure and High Temperature. Carbon is compressed within a metal cube and subjected to high heat and pressure using electric pulses. Over time, the carbon breaks down and forms a diamond through crystallisation.

body.text: What Is The Difference Between CVD And HPHT?

The most straightforward answer to this question is nothing. Both produce quality lab-grown diamonds, and it is not possible to distinguish which method produced the diamond. When purchasing a lab-grown diamond, you should not consider the process from which the diamond was grown. The production process of lab grown diamonds are now mostly produced in China and India. Due to cheap labor in these countries, lab grown stones are becoming very cost effective.
Benefits of Lab-Grown Diamonds

Lab-grown diamonds are more environmentally friendly, as their production does not involve the destructive mining processes that can harm ecosystems. They are also conflict-free, ensuring that they are not associated with human rights abuses or unethical practices. Furthermore, lab-grown diamonds can be produced using renewable energy sources, adding to their sustainability. Available in a range of qualities, from low to high, lab-grown diamonds cater to a wide array of consumer preferences and budgets.
How Do You Identify a Lab-Grown From a Natural Diamond?
Growth Patterns In Diamonds vs Naturally occurring diamonds.

While most of the primary growth factors of lab diamond growth are the same between lab and natural diamonds, they also have differences in their growth pattern. One big difference is the direction in which the diamonds grow, which can be detected with different tools and instruments, but those instruments are very expensive. Lab diamonds grow upward, and Earth diamonds grow outward from the centre.
Nitrogen Atoms In Lab Created Diamonds Not Present

The main distinguishing feature between lab diamonds and earth-created diamonds is that lab diamonds typically do not have nitrogen atoms in their molecular Matrix, while Earth-created diamonds usually do. However, a few natural diamonds also lack nitrogen atoms, making detection difficult.
Testing diamonds with Infrared Light Spectroscopy

A lab or jeweller can use infrared light spectroscopy to test a diamond to see if it has nitrogen within it. If the resulting spectroscopy graph shows a diamond has a nitrogen peak, it's almost certainly a real natural diamond. If the spectroscopy graph doesn't have nitrogen, then it likely is a lab diamond, but it could still be an Earth-created diamond that doesn't happen to have nitrogen. So, nitrogen's presence confirms natural diamonds, while its absence can't entirely rule out that it's a natural diamond.
Visual Differences to the Naked Eye between Lab Created Diamonds vs Mined Diamonds

While labs and special instruments can detect all of this, to the naked eye, **lab diamonds and Earth-created diamonds are visibly the same**. This means when anyone looks at them under normal lighting conditions without magnification, they cannot see the difference. They are both real diamonds, created differently, with slight differences. They even sparkle the same, with different cuts, carats, and clarities. In other words, they have microscopic flaws and are available in various shades and colours. So to just clarify, the human eye cannot see the differences. Unlike cubic zirconia, which are mere imitations, lab-grown diamonds are real diamonds with the same visual properties as natural diamonds.
Quality Grading Lab Grown Diamonds

Just like natural diamonds, lab-grown diamonds come in different variations of quality. This means both types should be graded and certified for quality so you don’t get ripped off. The so-called 4 Cs applied to grade natural diamonds are also applied to lab-grown diamonds via GIA or IGI certification. For example, clarity grades and colour grades are reported on. Lab created diamonds test as real diamonds according to standards set by authoritative organizations like the GIA.
Fluorescence Stones Likely Indicate Mined Diamonds

There are two scenarios where you can visibly tell the difference between some lab and some natural diamonds without professional equipment, in other words, with your natural eyes. When fluorescent light is on natural diamonds, if it has boron atoms in its Matrix, it will shine blue fluorescence. If it doesn't have boron in it, it will not shine at all with fluorescent light. It's a very cool phenomenon. If some lab-created diamonds have fluorescent light cast onto them, they will emit a more teal or orange colour or other random colours. They will also have different patterns of fluorescence. Sometimes, this will happen with Earth diamonds, but it is much more familiar with lab diamonds. So this is not necessarily a 100% rule, but if a diamond has fluorescence, it will likely be a natural diamond, and if it doesn't, it could be either. Still, you're now looking at the possibility of a lab diamond instead of with fluorescence; you aren't.
Phosphorescence

The second visible scenario is called phosphorescence. Some lab diamonds will continue to shine for a few moments after light is removed from them. This is phosphorescence. It, too, is rare, but it won't happen with natural diamonds at all.
Inclusions Under Magnification

Now, what about under magnification? Can you tell the difference? As I said earlier, all diamonds have variations in flaws, also called inclusions. Most of them can only be seen under magnification. You can notice a difference in those inclusions under magnification depending on how the lab diamonds were created. Lab diamonds can get this metallic flux in the inclusion or have a dark pinpoint inclusion, unlike natural diamonds.
Cost Comparison Between Lab Diamond and Natural Diamond

The cost is among the most significant differences between lab-grown and natural diamonds. For instance, a one-carat natural diamond with the highest colour and clarity (D, VVS2) costs around $10,000. On the other hand, a similar lab-grown diamond costs about $1,200. That's a significant difference!

body.alt: cost of lab grown diamonds.

body.text: Two-Carat Diamonds

Moving on to two-carat stones, a natural diamond with high colour and clarity can cost around $30,000. In contrast, a lab-grown diamond of similar quality costs about $2,000. Again, the price difference is staggering.
Three-Carat Diamonds

A three-carat natural stone can cost around $50,000, while a lab-grown diamond costs about $5,000. The price gap widens as the carat size increases, making lab-grown diamonds an attractive option for those looking to get more bang for their buck.
Four-Carat Diamonds

When comparing four-carat diamonds, a natural one costs around $90,000, while a lab-grown diamond costs about $7,500. The difference in price is even more pronounced, highlighting the affordability of lab-grown diamonds.
Six-Carat Diamonds

A natural six-carat diamond can cost around $140,000, while a lab-grown diamond costs about $9,500. The price difference is significant, but so are the quality and craftsmanship involved in creating these stones.
Finding a Quality Lab Diamond

Not all lab-grown diamonds are created equal, and there are a number of things to consider. HPHT diamonds are one type of lab-grown diamond that can vary in quality based on the growth process. How long the diamond was grown can significantly affect its quality, as can the quality of the gas, chemicals, and the growth recipe. Using cheaper-quality ingredients and shorter growth durations can leave undesirable results in the lab diamond. The characteristics we do not want in our lab-grown diamonds are tints and secondary colours, especially in colourless or near-colourless lab diamonds. We are checking to see that there are no blue, brown and grey tints in the stone. It can be more challenging for consumers to spot these tints in colour once the stone has been set in jewellery. At Aurora Saigon, we check our Lab-Grown diamonds for tints to ensure you get the best quality stone.

It is essential to understand that you must rely on more than just the GIA or IGI certificate to indicate the diamond’s quality. That goes for Lab-Grown diamonds and natural diamonds. Tints and secondary colours will not be mentioned in the certificates. Other none favourable characteristics you should look for that will not be mentioned in the certificate is the bow tie effect. Note that this only applies to elongated shapes like oval, marquise, and pear. Diamonds in round shapes do not suffer from this problem. Diamonds featuring a bow tie display dark, connected triangles in the centre of the diamond, creating a bow tie-shaped pattern. A noticeable bow tie effect is considered undesirable as it can detract from the beauty and brilliance of the diamond.
Things I Hate About Lab-Grown Diamonds. Let's bring up the negatives.

The number one thing I hate is the lack of resale value. Yes, lab diamonds do have less resale value, but I have a couple of things to discuss in that realm. So, yeah, it is true that if you walk into a jewellery store to try to sell your lab diamond, they will not be very interested. You are getting little back, even if they want to buy it. The interest just needs to be there. Some will say, I don’t even deal with labs. However, selling a natural diamond is by no means fun. Nobody gets a large portion back. You’re getting 50% back at best. If you go to a jewellery store or pawn shop, you usually get $0.20 on the dollar for most diamonds. So, yes, it has poor resale value because pawnshops and most jewellers will not want it. But honestly, even if it were a natural diamond, you would lose so much money. If this is a forever diamond or you plan on proposing, the resale should not be something that you worry about. Instead of selling, you could come to Aurora Saigon, and we will use your diamonds in a custom-made item for you.

body.alt: How are lab diamonds grown?

body.text: Additionally, lab-grown diamonds avoid the ethical and environmental issues associated with diamond mining.

The second thing I hate is that they're not as established. Okay, what does that mean? Lab diamonds recently became popular as an alternative to natural diamonds for many reasons, but they're still not established.

If you tell somebody, Oh, I’m looking at this lab diamond, they will say, a Lab diamond. What are you talking about? They’re going to have to attach a negative connotation to it immediately. And because it’s not established, it goes right into my next point. There’s a negative perception of a lab diamond because people don’t know about it. They don’t understand that it’s the same as a natural diamond. Chemically and optically. Perception is huge. The most significant negative is perception. It runs the world. It’s all about what people think, but because it’s not established, there could be a negative connotation and perception. But that perception is changing. In the last couple of years, it has skyrocketed for several reasons.

items: Affordability is number one.
It is environmentally friendly. It's nice to know that a diamond will not harm the environment, someone will not be taken advantage of, and child labour will not occur.

body.text: Those things are positives. But let's be honest: the most significant positive is money, right? It costs a lot less and is chemically and optically the same. This is especially true in these times when the economy is a little tighter and, you know, recessions are looming—more money for your kitchen, bathroom, or buying a house.

Money is important. Investing in the future is essential. If you're starting a life together, you want to have some money saved up. So, if the perception is slowly being altered, and that negative is slowly going to change, but as of right now, there is a perception to it that's negative. It's up to us to educate people so they understand the positives, and hey, you don't need to talk about it. You have a diamond ring on; you don't need to say, Hey, I am having a hard time because it's green, and it aligns with my values. I promise you, everyone's looking at lab diamonds right now because it just makes so damn much damn sense, right? So it is a negative perception. Wrong, but it's changing. A lot of people are coming around to it, including me. I love lab diamonds.
Limited Availability

Next is limited availability. Yes. You're going to need help finding lab-grown diamonds. Some people want to avoid buying online. The goal is to buy online because you're educated and understand; why spend more locally when you have more options online? When it comes to lab diamonds, you will be forced to go online because only some people have it locally. If they do, they're overpriced. Then you have a very limited quantity, and you'll pick from a handful of stones instead of picking from a thousand rocks and narrowing down your preferences. So, ideally, online is the way to go because you'll need more availability.
The Future of Lab-Grown Diamonds

The future of lab-grown diamonds looks promising as technology continues to advance and consumer preferences evolve. Lab-grown diamonds are gaining popularity among those seeking a more affordable, sustainable, and conflict-free alternative to natural diamonds. The diamond industry is adapting to this shift, with many companies investing in new technologies and production methods to meet the growing demand. Jewellers and retailers are increasingly recognising the value and quality of lab-grown diamonds, leading to wider acceptance and availability. As the demand for lab-grown diamonds continues to rise, they are poised to become an integral part of the diamond market, offering consumers a modern and ethical choice for their jewellery needs.
Preferences and Trends

Most women prefer size when it comes to diamonds. The bigger, the better. Lab-grown diamonds offer a way to get a larger stone for less money. However, many still prefer natural diamonds for significant purchases like a diamond engagement ring.

It's blingy, flashy, and beautiful. So, it is the reality of our world. Bigger is better. Even for a low budget, the chance to buy a beautiful one-carat diamond for an affordable price will never be a negative thing. And they're buying an actual diamond; whether it's lab or natural, it's chemically and optically the same.

body.text: What Colours Do Sapphires Come in?

If you want a precious stone but need help determining what colour you want, Sapphires has you covered. We have every shade from the most known and popular Blue sapphires to pinks, oranges, yellow, violet, green, black and colorless sapphires. Once the pinks start turning red, the stone is known as a Ruby. Ruby and Sapphires are in the same gemstone family, but Ruby does command a more significant price tag than Sapphires.

There are no limits to the tones and saturations of sapphires, and you will be amazed at just how many choices there are. What causes these differences in colour is the presence of different minerals in the gemstone. For example, blue sapphires have a titanium element with the stone. If chromium is present in the Sapphire, a pink colour will appear. A mixture of these chemicals in the crystal gives us variations in colours. Concerning white sapphires, these are classed as perfectly chemically pure. When it comes to colour, Mother Nature did spoil us with choice. A fun fact to remember: apart from the classic blue sapphires and white sapphires, coloured sapphires are known as fancy sapphires.
Sapphire Hardness and Crystal Structure

If you didn't know, gemstones are measured for their hardness by the Mohs scale (pronounced MOZE). The Good news is that Sapphires are pretty tough cookies and come in at 9 out of 10. This means they are great for everyday wear and are a very durable stone. Another reason why Sapphires make great engagement rings. To learn more about the Mohs scale and hardness of gemstones, visit GIA article on Mohs.
Origin of Sapphires

Ruby and sapphire are varieties of corundum and corundum is found abundantly all over the world. However, gemstone quality corundum is exceptionally rare. The actual origins of a Sapphire play a big part in the value of the stone, so it is important to know about the origins of sapphires when buying. Understanding where a Sapphire came from can be quite difficult, but gemologist can usually identify where it was mined from by the inclusions within the stone.

From our opinion, the best Sapphires are from Sri Lanka, Nigeria and Madagascar, as these Sapphires tend to have more lusture and brightness about them. Listed below are a few interesting locations where gemstone quality sapphires originate from.

body.alt: Sapphire Buying Guide - Aurora Saigon, Vietnam - Precious Blue Sapphire Gemstone Close-up

body.text: Sri Lanka a.k.a Ceylon Sapphires
Sri Lanka historically was called Ceylon from its colonial days. Sapphires from Sri Lanka are known as Ceylon Sapphires and are found in many colours and sizes, except for the colour indigo.

Sri Lanka boasts some of the oldest mines for Sapphires recording back to the 4th and 5th century AD. Not only are Sapphires mined such a long time ago from Sri Lanka but to the global market today, Sri Lanka is one of the largest suppliers of Sapphires.

Ceylon Sapphires come in many types of colours, but the sort after light blue colour, which is a true cobalt blue, are much distinguishable from dark blue sapphires from Thailand and Australia. For this reason blue Ceylon Sapphires are more expensive, ranging from $200 to $9000, depending on the 4 c's.

body.alt: rare pinkish orange sapphires from sri lanka and madagascar

body.text: The Padparadscha Sapphire

These unique sapphires are a blend of pink and orange and even though Parparadscha sapphires can be found in other locations, Sri Lanka is considered the true origin of this type of Sapphire. The colour is a delicate mix of pinkish-orange hues, and is said to resemble the tips of a new lotus flower at dawn. Padmaraga is a Sanskrit term for lotus blossom, which is where Padparadscha Sapphires derive their name from. These types of sapphires command a higher price because of their desirability and are the rarest and most expensive Sapphires.

body.alt: Sapphire Buying Guide - Aurora Saigon, Vietnam - Raw Blue Sapphire

body.text: Kashmir Sapphires

High quality Sapphires are found in Northen India, Kashmir, but the mines are now considered depleted and closed. For this reason, no new sapphires are appearing on the market from Kashmir, which makes older Sapphires from this region expensive.

Kashmir sapphires are generally cloudy but offer an extremely attractive blue colour. Stones from Kashmir are highly sort after. Due to the fact no new Kashmir sapphires are entering the market, this origin of sapphire will likely not be an option to you.

body.alt: ILAKAKA, MADAGASCAR - AUGUST 2017: aerial view of poor African people looking for gold, precious gems, sapphires in a muddy river near Ilakaka, Ihorombe region, Madagascar

body.text: Madagascar Sapphires

Large deposits of Sapphires were found only as recently as 1998 in Madagascar. Finding large deposits is exceptionally rare in this day and age. The colour Sapphires that are mainly found in Madagascar are from yellow, pink, green, white, and the infamous orange Padparadscha Sapphire.

body.text: Cambodian Sapphires

Sapphires from Cambodia have dark, smokey hues and are mined from the Pailin and Preah Vihar provinces. Unfortunately, the Sapphires from Pailin have a dark history with their connection to funding the Khmer Rouge regime. They were one of the first blood gemstones. Today, in more peaceful times, Sapphires from Cambodia are being mined again. Typically, the Sapphires that come out of Pailin are on the small side. Also, this type of colour sapphire, with its dark blues, is not for everyone, but it can make for an exciting piece.

body.alt: yellow sapphire Gemstone close up Shot

body.text: Vietnam Sapphires

Seems we are a Vietnamese-based company; it would be rude not to mention the beautiful colored stones that can be found in Vietnam. Sapphires and Rubies can be found in the following areas in Vietnam: the Central Highlands provinces of Dak Lak and Lam Dong, as well as the southern provinces of Dong Nai and Binh Thuan. Most of the mining is performed by small-scale, independent operators. Most of this rough material ends up across borders in nearby Thailand for cutting, so the origins of Vietnamese Sapphires can be lost, and a true understanding of the quality of Sapphires coming out of Vietnam. The gemstone quality and large deposits of Corundum are considered promising for the future of Vietnam.
Star Sapphires

A star sapphire could also take your interest. This sort after stone, which appears as though a star is trapped inside, makes for a captivating stone. The optical phenomenon is known as asterism, which is the Latin meaning for star. What makes the star effect in star sapphires? Needle-like inclusions of the mineral rutile within the gemstone, although in black sapphires the star effect is caused by the mineral hematite. Do note though, that this optical phenomenon only appears when light is shined onto the gemstone, else the stone will appear dark and opaque.

body.text: Blue Sapphire Engagement Ring

One lady and one lady alone made Blue Sapphire engagement rings popular: Princess Diana! Picking a Blue sapphire for her engagement ring was seen as stepping outside the norm. Princess Diana was a lady known not to follow the crowd or what was expected. Now the most famous engagement ring in the world, Blue Sapphires are an excellent choice for an engagement ring. It doesn't always have to be diamonds for an engagement ring. However, diamonds do compliment Blue Sapphires exceptionally well. If you are looking to create a custom Blue Sapphire Engagement ring, contact us and check out our Custom Engagement Ring process.

body.text: How to Buy Blue Sapphire

The Sapphire's colour is the main influence in its value. The best quality blue sapphires have a very vivid saturation and medium dark tones. Sky blue sapphires and dark blue command a lower value. Look for a velvety blue sapphire, which is known as royal blue sapphire.
Cornflower Sapphire

A perfectly blue sapphire is very rare, known in the trade as cornflower blue sapphires. These are expensive sapphires due to their rarity and are highly prized. Why the name Cornflower? It is based on the colour of the Cornflower. This flower contains a distinct blue hue, and the name was given because these flowers were prominent in cornfields. Thus, the ability of a natural gemstone to capture this elusive colour and particular shade of blue makes it a high-value proposition in terms of rarity and beauty.

body.alt: Cornflower blue - perfect blue gem colour

body.text: Most Popular Sapphire Stone Cuts
The most popular stone cuts for Sapphires, and the easiest cuts to find on the market are the following,

items: Cushion cut
Round cut
Oval cut
Emerald cut

body.alt: blue sapphire stone cuts

body.text: The round-shaped cut Sapphire is probably the most popular but tends to be the most expensive per carat weight. This style of cut is not the most economical, resulting in more waste than other cuts.

An Oval cut is a classic shape for engagement sapphire rings. Natural sapphires cut in this shape make the stone look more significant than other sapphires of the same weight. This elegant, timeless shape will give the illusion that your fingers are more prolonged.
A Cushion shaped Sapphire can also make for a great cut for an engagement ring.

Choosing a shape for you depends on whether you want to make a strong statement with, say, an unusual heart or marquise cut or keep it traditional with a round and oval stone. Most importantly, whatever shape you pick is a personal choice that can have meaning and the one you love the most.
Synthetic Sapphires

Sapphire was one of the first gemstones to be lab-grown and synthesised due to the fact that gem-quality Sapphires are rarer than diamonds and demand far exceeds natural supply. It is important to understand that a synthetic blue sapphire is not a fake Sapphire. By every means, they are optically, chemically and structurally identical to natural sapphires. Synthetic sapphires are obviously a lot cheaper than natural stones, so it is important to know if the stone is man made. When inspecting a synthetic sapphire you will see little to no inclusions within the stone and it will be of exceptional quality. If the prices is too good to be true, it normally is. If in doubt, always seek a gem report.
Sapphire Treatments

Treated Sapphires are generally the norm, and the majority of commercial-grade Sapphires have had some kind of treatment. There has been a long history of practises of treating sapphires to give them more vivid colors and improving a Sapphire's clarity. With todays modern technology, practices have improved some what.

body.alt: The Good, The Bad and the ugly of Sapphire Treatment Guide

body.text: Heat Treated (Good)

Heat treatment is the more common treatment for Sapphires and for most other gemstones for that mater. As the name suggests, the gemstone is heated to a very high temperature. By heating the Sapphire you can change the colour to a more desirable colour, either by developing or intensifying its natural colour. The more aggressive the heating the less value the Sapphire becomes.

Heat treatment can also improve the clarity of the stone by removing or reducing the inclusions in the stone. In the trade heat treatments are considered acceptable, as they are a stable treatment and permanent. Slightly heat treated stones can also command high ct weight prices, upwards to $3,000 a ct.
Radiation Treatments (Bad)

This is another treatment that is also used to improve the colour of a stone. However, radiation is not a stable treatment, unlike heat treatments; over time, the gemstone colour will fade if exposed to bright light or heat. You will find this treatment mostly applied to fancy sapphires, turning pale colours into more vivid colours.
Fracture Filling Treatments (Ugly)

The worst treatment is the fracture filling treatment. Exceptionally poor quality corundum is injected with lead glass to fill in the fractures of the stone. This type of treatment is unstable, and you should not waste your money on such poor-quality stones.

Our experience in Vietnam is that these treatments are not disclosed to the buyer, which is disappointing, mainly since we have found glass-filled rubies and sapphires being sold by significant well-known high street brands in Vietnam that are not being disclosed, and to make things worse, at unfair prices.

It is essential to understand that when buying a fracture-filled Sapphire, it is impossible to know how much of it is glass and how much of it is Sapphire (corundum). So much so that a gemological institute would class the gemstone as a 'composite' stone, with no mention of Sapphire. The value of these lead glass filled Sapphires and Rubies is about $30 ct and in our opinion is only suitable for cheap silver jewellery.

If you are going to invest your hard earned money in a Sapphire, we recommend a lab report from gemological institute, like GIA or any other trusted gemological institute. This way you can be confident you know about any treatments the stone has had.
Beryllium Diffusion (Controversial)

When heat treatment fails to improve the colour of the stone, another treatment called Beryllium Diffusion is used. The stone is heated to its near melting point and then diffused into the stone with the element beryllium. This colour-inducing element penetrates deep with stone to bring a more vivid color.

The practice is somewhat controversial within the industry because it can be hard to detect, and many of these treated sapphires have been mistaken for natural padparadschas sapphires. However, in recent years, it has now become easier for trained gemologists to detect.
The good news about the Beryllium diffusion treatment is that it is entirely stable, and for stones that have had this treatment, the new colour is consistently distributed through the Sapphire.
After the Sapphire has had this type of treatment, the stone is considerably cheaper in value and is offered in the trade considerably cheaper than stones without it.
How to Care for Sapphire

To clean your sapphire we recommend using warm soupy water and a gemstone cleaning cloth. When the sapphire is set in jewellery use a soft toothbrush to clean through the setting. Do not use chemicals to clean your stone.
Sapphires are the second hardest gemstone, second only to diamond. They very rarely crack, scratch or chip due to corundum being incredibly tough.

When storing your jewellery, please separate them careful and make sure they do not touch each other. Some stones will scratch others, for example Emeralds, Opals and Tanzanites are a much softer stone, so can be scratched easily.

It is also essential to know that a treated natural sapphire should be cared for even more due to its potentially unstable condition not taking too kindly to heat and other factors. When sending your Jewellery with a treated sapphire to a goldsmith, it is vital to inform them of the stone treatment so no cleaning processes or work can be carried out that may damage the stone. If your Sapphire has only been heat treated, you should not worry, but all other treatments can be a concern.
Sapphire History, Lore and Fun Facts
Sapphires have been steeped in mystery and lore for many centuries. This stone has been associated with royalty, religion and romance, captivating the world with its beauty.
Blue Sapphires have always be the standard by which other blue gemstones, like Tanzanite and Blue Topaz, have been measured against.

The name Sapphire originates from the greek word sappheiros, and for those lucky ones born in September, Sapphire is your birthstone. Also this stone celebrates the fifth and forty fifth wedding anniversaries, so why no celebrate these occasions with a sapphire ring!
Conclusion

With this sapphire buying guide, we aim to cover all aspects that will help you make an informed purchase of a Sapphire. But when purchasing expensive sapphires or any expensive gemstone, you are also buying into the seller. It is essential to get to know the individual seller as well as the item you are purchasing. This is why at Aurora Saigon, we make the time and effort to inform our customers as much as possible about gemstones and jewellery and not just looking to sell. This exquisite gemstone, known for its stunning spectrum of blue and violet hues, holds a special place in the hearts of those born in December and is an emblem of celebration for couples marking their 24th wedding anniversary. Yet, there's so much more to Tanzanite than meets the eye.

body.text: What Is The Magical Tanzanite All About?

Tanzanite is a highly scarce gemstone that is not as popular as diamonds but is exquisite and owned by few people worldwide. They are so rare that they can only be found in the deep foothills of Mount Kilimanjaro. The location of this gemstone and the fact that it is rarely found has made it one of the most charming and coveted jewels for collectors.

Naturally, Tanzanite is a type of crystal called zoisite and considered the most well known of zoisite crystals. Tanzanite is the trade name for blue zoisite and was given by Tiffany & Co, as they thought zoisite not being a perfect marketing name. The colour of this gemstone comes from the appearance of vanadium while forming. Tanzanite is the most famous blue stone other than the blue sapphires, so they are a rare find and one of the most beautiful finds. Due to the rare, occurring nature of the gemstone, these are referred to as a 'geological phenomenon.'
Where are Tanzanites Mined?

These stones are mined in tiny areas in the foothill of Mount Kilimanjaro. The distance is about two km in length and four km in width. The area where this occurs is known as the Manyara Region of Northern Tanzania. However, geologists have stated that these stunning Tanzanite gemstones are exquisite because their formation over 585 million years ago was exceptional.

Tanzanite was found over seven decades ago in 1967 and was declared by Tiffany & Co to be the most exquisite stone ever discovered in the past 2000 years. However, the initial discovery of the crystal was by the Maasai tribespeople, who had no interest in the crystal and saw it as having little value.
No other stone can compare to its beauty, mainly because it is a trichoic stone. It reflects mixed colours ranging from mild blues to shades of purples.

What Colours Does The Tanzanite Display?

Tanzanite is the same as all the other blue gemstones, and it occurs naturally in a spectrum of different hues. The range, however, differs, and these Tanzanite stones have the deepest blues to pale violet. One of the most desired tanzanite gemstone colours is deep blue, covered by a tint of purple.

Yet, that is not the only reason why tanzanite stone is unique. It is also because it is the only known stone to showcase multidimensional colour. In simpler words, you see three different colours when this magical stone is seen from three different directions. It can show you a deep blue colour, violet on the other, and sometimes even red on the third side. This phenom is referred to as trichroic.

body.text: Tanzanite Gemstones Are A Rarer Find Than Diamonds

Diamond is the most famous and loved gemstone worldwide. They are of utmost significance and are given at the most special occasions, such as weddings and graduations. They are also known to represent the 60th anniversary. There is no doubt that a diamond is rare, and its value differs based on its size and colour.

However, tanzanite gemstones are, without a doubt, rarer than diamonds. They say up to 1000 times more rarer than a diamond. It is because the chances of finding these beautiful Tanzanites are less. And now, considering that the global supply is likely to be depleted within the next 25 years makes, it an even more unique stone. If you're looking for a stunning statement stone to blow away the love of your life, or you wish to have a secure investment, you can't go wrong with a tanzanite gemstone.

But why do Tanzanites not command the same monetary value as diamonds? This is because Tanzanite crystals are not as hard as diamonds, where a Tanzanite comes in on the Mohs scale at 6 1/2. It is much softer than most gemstones, so wearing it requires more care. It is also not in as much demand as diamonds. Also, Tanzanite can be found in large carat sizes easier, whereas Diamonds are rarer in large sizes that are flawless and of good quality.
Tanzanite Treatment - Heat Treated

Around 96% of Tanzanites are heat treated, and only 4% are not. This treatment is considered safe and acceptable within the jewellery trade, as the treatment is stable and permanent. If your Tanzanite gemstone has been heat treated, chances are it has; it will only display two colours, blue and violet. However, if the Tanzanite gemstone has three colours, it may not be heat treated, or it may have been lightly heated. We cannot be 100% sure, even if the stone has three colours. Cut

Colour

Clarity

When we talk about a gemstone's clarity, we refer to the inclusions and flaws within the stone. These are natural imperfections within the crystal that mother nature added. The inclusions' size, how many inclusions the stone carries, location of faults affect the gemstone's value. Grading of clarity is similar to how we grade diamonds. IF represents internally flawless and rocks containing inclusions ranging from VVS, VS, SI, I. You will find very few Tanzanite Jewellery comes with a certificate. The inclusions will likely not be visible to the human eye, and magnification 6 times is required to see them.

Whether you're attracted to its stunning color palette, intrigued by its history, or drawn to its spiritual significance, one thing is certain: owning a piece of Tanzanite is like having a piece of Earth's history. Can rose quartz go in water?

Can rose quartz crystals go in water? The answer to that question is not a simple yes or no. While some people may argue that they have had success with placing their rose quartz crystal in water, this is not recommended as it can cause damage to the stone.

Rose quartz is a beautiful pink-colored gemstone that has been used for centuries for its calming and healing properties. Rose quartz is widely used in jewelry and home decor today, but what many don't realize is that it can be very sensitive to water.

The problem with placing a rose quartz crystal in water lies in its composition. Rose quartz consists of silicon dioxide (SiO2), which has tiny cracks and fissures on its surface that are invisible to the human eye. Over time, these cracks can become filled with moisture, allowing rust and other contaminants to form inside the stone. This can lead to permanent discoloration or even change the structure of the stone over time.

Additionally, some types of rose quartz contain small amounts of iron or manganese, which are metals prone to rusting when exposed to water. This process can cause staining or dullness on its surface, making it look less than desirable compared to how it originally looked before being submerged in water.

It's possible that some forms of rose quartz crystals may be able to withstand being placed in water for short periods of time without any damage occurring; however, there is no guarantee as every form of rose quartz will likely react differently when exposed to moisture over time. Therefore, it's best not to risk it by placing your rose quartz gemstones or crystals into water as it could end up causing irreparable damage instead of providing any benefits from doing so.
Can rose quartz be in the sun?
Do:

If you want to charge your rose quartz crystal with sun exposure, it is important to place rose quartz in a shady area out of direct sunlight. This allows the stone to be exposed to the positive effects of natural sunlight without its harmful UV rays. Ensure there are no obstructions between the sun and your crystal like trees or overhangs to prevent any interruption in its energy charging process.
Don't:

Avoid exposing your rose quartz crystal directly to intense sunlight, particularly if the piece is fragile or cracked. Direct exposure to UV radiation causes further cracking and damage, while also discoloring and weakening its composition over time. Additionally, avoid leaving it outside overnight as this can reduce the efficacy of its charging power due to weather changes and other external factors such as wind and moisture.
Conclusion:

When looking for effective sun-charging for you rose quartz crystal, make sure you are aware of both what you should do and what you should not do. body.text: Have you ever seen a piece of jewelry with an incredibly bright, reflective white color? Chances are it was rhodium plated. Rhodium plating is used to add lustre and shine to jewelry pieces made from gold, silver, or platinum. It’s part of the platinum metal family and is much harder than gold, providing jewelry with a durable surface that resists scratches and tarnishes. Rhodium is also rarer and more expensive than gold, 6.6 times more expensive, as of Feb 2023! Everything you need to know about rhodium plating is right here! This blog post will take a closer look at rhodium plating and how it can be used for various types of jewelry.

body.text: What is the metal Rhodium?

In 1803, William Hyde Wollaston discovered a precious metal that had eluded the eyes of humankind for centuries - rhodium! It was named after the **Greek word 'rhodon'**, which translates to mean rose due to its coloration in solution. Not only did he discover this one-of-a-kind substance but also palladium in 1802. An even more remarkable fact is that it can only be encountered as traces within platinum or nickel ores, and **80% of it comes from South Africa** - with production numbers at an incredible **20 tons annually** - talk about rare!

body.text: The Benefits of Rhodium Plating

Rhodium plating has several benefits that make it popular among jewelry makers and consumers. It makes any jewelry look brighter, shinier, and more expensive without using pure gold or platinum metals. It also provides **superior protection** against wear-and-tear damage, making the piece longer-lasting and more durable overall. Plus, rhodium plating easily adheres to different types of metals, such as sterling silver or white gold alloys.
How Long Does Rhodium Plating Last?

The lifespan of rhodium plating depends on several factors, including the type of metal being used (gold vs silver vs platinum), the quality of the original metal alloy being used in the piece (14K gold vs 18K gold), and how often the item is worn (daily vs occasional). Generally speaking, though, most rhodium-plated pieces will **last anywhere from 1-3 years** before needing to be re-plated again, depending on their usage rate.
Will Rhodium Plating Affect Gemstones?

When working with softer gemstones such as **opals, pearls, coral, or turquoise**, extra caution must be taken during the rhodium plating process, as these stones are more delicate. Sterling silver does not need rhodium plating to achieve a bright white colour; however, sterling silver can still tarnish over time, which is why many people opt for rhodium-plated pieces for added protection **against oxidation or discolouration** over time. We at Aurora Saigon rhodium plate all our silver to ensure your investment in our jewelry lasts.
How Long Does Rhodium Plating Take to Do?

Our workshops are dedicated to giving you the fastest turn-around possible - often, **same-day rhodium plating** service is available! So no matter how much work we have, your pieces can be quickly and professionally handled.

When it comes to rhodium plating, the biggest downside is its cost. body.text: Rhodium plating process

If you're wondering about the methods of adding a layer of rhodium plating, a goldsmith uses an **electroplating machine** to add this precious metal. The perfect thickness is **.75-1.0 microns** - which might sound thin but provides ample protection against abrasions when used on jewelry items subject to rough wear and tear.

Jewelers must ensure their jewelry is in **pristine condition** before rhodium plating. Even the tiniest speck of dirt can prevent a successful coating, so standard cleaning protocols are not enough - they require extra attention and care to truly shine through on each piece! Electrocleaning is one treatment that delivers optimal cleanliness, involving polishing methods followed by an ultrasonic power steam rinse, and this process will guarantee any debris or impurities hindering the application of Rhodium are carefully cleared away for perfect results.
